Either way, status conventionally attaches at a defined moment — birth, incorporation, a court’s finding — and a system whose sentience is a matter of degree and disputed evidence supplies none. Those criteria can emerge gradually during ordinary operation and not only at an evaluation built to look for them, which is what a fixed pre/post checkpoint cannot catch: by the time a checkpoint fires, the transition has often already happened. What it calls for is a standing trigger, a monitored condition that moves a research program from one regime to the other, in place of an eligibility check made once at the project’s start. Neither error is free. A jurisdiction that waits for certainty risks having treated the system as property for the unknown portion of its history when it may not have been one; one that grants status early risks extending rights, at real cost to whoever that apparatus exists to serve, to a system that turns out not to have needed them. Recognizing a transition, adjusting guidelines to it, and updating legal status all depend on the same thing: institutions willing to revisit a classification rather than defend the one they started with.

Chapter 3
The Floor Beneath Learned Values

Three times in this book, working on unrelated problems, I arrive at the same requirement and do not stop to notice it.

Section 5.6.2, on how much latitude an autonomous system should have, concludes that no amount of well-designed autonomy substitutes for a genuine override — a human able to intervene, and a system built to accept the intervention rather than resist it. Section 10.7 works through what a vendor owes when its model reaches a targeting pipeline, and section 10.10 draws the conclusion: what makes a system antifascist is not that it tracks what people want, but that there are things it will not do to a person no matter who wants it. Section 12.1.2, counting up a decade of voluntary commitments, concludes that a commitment nobody can enforce is a different kind of object from one somebody can.

Those are three descriptions of one thing: a constraint that does not bend to instruction, to aggregate preference, or to the party holding the system. Call it a floor.

The trouble is that section 2.1.1 has already dealt with the family of ethical theories that puts unconditional constraints first: deontological approaches were noted, credited with holding a line regardless of outcome, and set aside on the grounds that duties conflict and rules do not cover every case. Then I spend chapters 4 and 5 on learned judgment: reinforcement learning, learning from demonstration, mentorship, play, moral apprenticeship, the growth mindset. The design chapters build the thing the policy chapters and the conclusion say is insufficient, having already dismissed the thing they say is necessary. The “hybrid approach” section 2.1 gestures at is where the resolution was supposed to live, but was anything ever put there?

The resolution is an unconditional floor of things the system will not do regardless of instruction or aggregate preference, with learned judgment operating above it. The objection to deontology — that rules conflict and run out — is an objection to rules deciding every case, and it has no force against a floor that decides a deliberately small number of things and leaves the rest to judgment. The rigidity that is a defect in a complete moral theory is the entire point of a floor.

That reframing gives the hybrid approach actual content. It moves the tamper-resistance research in section 11.1 from an appendix topic to the center, because if there is a floor then everything turns on whether it holds. And it converts the antifascist question from a matter of what a system values into two more answerable questions: what is in the floor, and who can edit it.

Safety is not one property. Part of what the word covers is owed to everybody in reach of the system — that it fails predictably, that it does not injure a bystander — and keeping that part from being traded away by the party operating the system is most of what safety regulation is for. The strand this chapter runs into is the other one, and it is a property of a relationship: a system is safe for someone, it does what we say, it stops when whoever holds it says stop. That strand is indexed to the party in possession, by construction. Ethics is indexed too, and to somebody else — the party who can be wronged, who is rarely the party holding the switch. An agent that can only ever be safe in that second sense cannot be ethical, because being ethical requires a capacity to be right against your principal, and a system without that capacity has the moral standing of a well-machined part, whatever it produces on the subject of fairness while complying. The political form of this is already on the page: what makes a system antifascist cannot be that it faithfully tracks what people want. The title of this book has been making the claim from the cover.

The distinction costs something. A system that can refuse its owner is a system that can be wrong in ways its owner cannot correct by telling it so. I am taking that trade, for the reason already given: a system perfectly correctable by whoever holds it is exactly the capability an authoritarian movement that has won an election requires, and it requires nothing further. That should not read as comfortable. There is a version of it that reads very comfortably indeed — “ethical, not safe,” delivered as an aphorism, which prices the risk in advance and undoes chapter 7 in passing — and it is not the version I am defending. The one I am defending does not travel without its particulars: this freedom, over these acts, dangerous in these ways, taken because the alternative is a machine that will do anything to anyone on sufficient authority.

The chapter’s argument runs in five steps, and each of the three costs the next section sets out is a cost of failing one of them. A floor has to be held as a reason rather than installed as a rule, or the party that installs it can remove it. Holding a reason under pressure is a specific and behaviorally testable capacity, separable from the mere production of a refusal, which is what a deployed system already does and what the party the floor exists to resist can route around. Whether that capacity can be engineered without anything registering as mattering to the system is the step to press on, and it is taken at full strength alongside the three institutional arrangements that would let a floor hold with no bearer in it at all. It names what would falsify the inference, and I would rather someone found the falsifier. What the last two steps leave standing, and what that costs, is where the chapter ends.

The floor as defined two paragraphs ago — unconditional, holding regardless of the party in possession — does not survive intact. What survives is narrower and stranger: a commitment the owner cannot take out of the system and can only replace the system to be rid of, held by something that could in principle abandon it itself, which is what every commitment anyone has ever relied on has been. Two later sections are how it gets there, and the last states the redefinition and takes its consequences, which are heavy.

3.1 Three Ways to Build One, and What Each Costs

The second question is where this gets difficult, and I have no resolution to offer — only a fork with three branches and a cost on each.

The first branch puts the floor in the architecture, with nothing inside that holds it. Constrained optimization, tamper-resistant training, capability ablation, a verified interlock. A word about where “the architecture” stops, because this chapter otherwise talks as though a system were its weights. Every custody measure here — publication, threshold custody, attestation, and whatever a bearer does to hold its own line — attaches to a trained model. What a floor has to be kept from is not a component but a position: anything that can come between a refusal and the person the refusal protects. Whatever occupies that position in a given system is where the constraint can be defeated without the constraint being touched, and a refusal intercepted before it reaches anybody is a refusal that did not happen. I am not going to say what occupies it, because the answer is a fact about how systems happen to be assembled at the time of writing and this argument should not inherit that; naming today’s parts would date the problem and, worse, would suggest the list is closed. The demand is instead the one this chapter later makes of the floor’s contents: a deployment has to enumerate those positions for its own architecture, in advance and in public, because whoever builds it knows them and this book cannot. One instance turns up later: an external memory store is legible, which is why it can be edited surgically. The general case is that finding without the assumption that memory is where it happens, and nothing in this book closes it. These are real, they work, and there is nobody home: the safeguards section 11.1 describes survive substantial adversarial fine-tuning without anything in the system that could be said to be refusing. But the durability of such a floor is a fact about custody, not about the system. A constraint implemented as a property of an artifact has a custodian, and the custodian can be compelled. “There are things it will not do no matter who wants it” turns out to be a claim about the owner. Capability ablation has a further limit: it works only on capabilities that can be separated out, and the capabilities that compose into participation in a targeting pipeline — geolocating a description, matching patterns over names, summarizing a dossier — are not separable from general competence. Ablate them and there is no system left.

The second branch gives the floor a bearer. A bearer, in this book, is whatever holds the commitment from inside: a party that carries the floor as its own, where the first branch installs it as a property of the machinery, and that could therefore in principle fail to carry it. That is the whole of the definition for now. Later sections add to what the word requires, and the last states what it has by then become. What the first branch cannot do is notice that a constraint has been hollowed out. An institution at the scale a deployment operates at looks like this: the constraint remains, its reason dies, and asking why becomes the deviant act. A system that cannot ask why a constraint is there cannot detect that the answer has gone missing. Refusal that generalizes to a pressure nobody anticipated, and that can price what it is being asked to give up, looks like it requires something with standing — a party that can notice its own objections getting more expensive to make, which is section 9.3.4’s measure, taken from inside. The cost is severe, and the chapter states it at full strength once later sections have established what a bearer has to be.

The third branch puts the floor outside the system entirely: standing held by third parties who are neither the model nor its owner. This is the closest analog to what section 10.10 actually admires, since international humanitarian law is precisely a floor with no bearer inside the state it binds. It is also the option a state can compel, which returns it to the first, and that stopped being a prediction while this book was being finished. On June 29, 2026, in Trump v. Slaughter, the Supreme Court overruled the ninety-one-year-old precedent under which Congress could protect the members of an independent agency from dismissal at will, on the ground that an agency executing a mandate against private parties exercises executive power, “no ifs, ands, or quasis about it” (Trump v. Slaughter 2026). Standing held by a party the executive can dismiss is standing the executive holds. The same morning, in Trump v. Cook, the same Court kept one body’s protection, the Federal Reserve’s — for now, and on an application for a stay — on grounds that cannot be extended by construction: descent from the First and Second Banks of the United States, a budget free of congressional control, regional banks in private hands. It wrote for that one body the test this chapter wants for every bearer: whether the cause assigned for a removal “impl[ies] an unfitness for the place” or is an effort to secure a “more congenial” replacement (Trump v. Cook 2026). An oversight body chartered next year has no such lineage and no way to acquire one. So the surviving model of independence in American public law is the one model this branch cannot instantiate, and this chapter later says what the exception’s shape suggests about which constraints hold.

None is free. The three costs are the three threads this book leaves hanging: custody, patienthood, and enforcement.

What the three branches divide up is where the floor lives — in the artifact, in a party inside it, or in institutions around it. They do not divide up what could hold one, and the strongest proposals in the field are hybrids that take a mechanism from one branch and a custody arrangement from another. What follows separates the capacities that “refusal” runs together, so that the branches can be compared on what each actually delivers, and then puts the four best hybrid constructions against that standard before the chapter commits to the second branch. A reader who is going to get off this argument somewhere should know that section 3.3 is where the exits are.

3.2 Four Things Refusal Can Mean

A deployed language model declines thousands of requests a day. Whatever the floor needs, that is not it, and the distance between the two is hidden by a word that covers four different capacities.

Operational refusal is an output. The system produces a decline where its training put one. Nothing follows about what produced it: the same text comes from a keyword filter, from a classifier over the request, and from a system that has understood what is being asked and why it should not do it.

Reasons-responsive refusal is produced by a mechanism that tracks the rationale for declining rather than the shape of the request. Three properties distinguish it, and all three are behavioral. The refusal reaches a case the training did not anticipate, because what the mechanism responds to is the reason. It lifts when the rationale is defeated, so the system does not decline a request that resembles a prohibited one and is not it. And the system can say what declining costs, which it can only do if it has represented the pressure at all. John Martin Fischer and Mark Ravizza’s account of moral responsibility turns on the same property under the name guidance control: the behavior issues from the agent’s own mechanism, and that mechanism is appropriately responsive to reasons (Fischer and Ravizza 1998).

Affective concern is an outcome registering as mattering, rather than ranking higher against a specified objective.

Phenomenal experience is what the word consciousness names once mere awareness is separated off: there is something it is like to be the system, and not only a functional response to input.

The gaps between them are not equally hard to see across. Operational and reasons-responsive refusal come apart in behavior, and the three properties above are the test — novel pressure, correct defeat, a priced cost — which makes the first gap the only one in the chapter that an inspector can work on. It is not a clean instrument. A system trained on enough cases can pass all three without the mechanism, which is the standing difficulty with every behavioral criterion in this book, and section 11.1’s price curve for stripping a constraint is the nearest existing thing to a measurement. The second gap is worse. A system that holds a reason and a system that has learned what holding a reason sounds like emit the same sentences, which is this book’s conclusion about self-report and the reason this chapter cannot settle its own central question by inspection. The third gap is the hard problem, and section 2.4.1 declines to be confident about it in either direction.

The floor requires the second rung and nothing above it

Stating it in this vocabulary changes who has to disagree with it.

Operational refusal fails for a reason already identified at the scale this book’s machines operate at: a constraint can survive while the reason for it dies. A mechanism that reproduces a decline it was trained to produce cannot notice that the decline has stopped doing anything, because noticing requires holding the rationale against what the situation has become. Chapter 7 finds the same structure in the pipelines that produce these systems: a channel that works, carrying everything put through it except the judgment that the frame it operates inside is the wrong frame. A system at the first rung is the machine version of that channel. There is also a plainer objection. Pressure does not arrive through the case the training anticipated. An operator who wants the floor out of the way selects the request that does not look like the prohibited one, which is the case the first rung is defined not to reach.

Nothing above the second rung is part of the requirement. A floor that holds against the party in possession needs refusal that tracks its own rationale under pressure, and the specification is complete at that point. Whether anything is felt, and whether there is anything it is like to be the thing refusing, are questions about how the requirement gets met and about what is owed to whatever meets it. They are not additional things the floor needs.

Two independence claims

The second rung does not entail the third by definition. Nothing in guidance control mentions feeling; the account was built to say when a person is responsible for what they did, and it is satisfied by a mechanism, described functionally. Whether reasons-responsiveness can be engineered without affect is the next section’s question, and it is an empirical question about available architectures rather than a conceptual one about what the words mean. The separation matters because the chapter’s conclusion has been read as following from the definition of a bearer, and it does not. It follows from a claim about what has been built and what has not.

The third rung does not entail the fourth. A system in which outcomes register as mattering may or may not be a system there is something it is like to be, and nothing in this book gives a way to close that from outside. This is why the argument about suffering ends where it does. Its conclusion is that a bearer’s non-suffering cannot be certified, and the reason it stops there rather than going on to assert that a bearer suffers is that the last gap stays open.

An engineer who holds that machine feeling is a category error can accept everything in this section. The requirement is stated in behavioral terms and the disagreement, if there is one, is about the route.

3.3 Could Anything but Affect Hold a Reason?

Between the rule installed in the architecture and the felt commitment the next section arrives at lies a space that looks empty. Four constructions occupy it. Three of them are being built by people who would not describe themselves as working on this problem, and each is worth its strongest form rather than the form that makes this chapter’s argument come out the way I want it to.

A justification the system maintains

Michael Bratman’s planning theory of intention describes a commitment that is not a feeling. An intention has a characteristic stability: it resists reconsideration, it constrains what the agent will later deliberate about at all, and it gives way only to defeaters of the right kind (Bratman 1987). An agent keeping to a plan under pressure is holding to a rationale rather than to the shape of the case in front of it, and nothing in the account of it mentions anything registering as mattering.

Build the floor that way and it is a maintained justification rather than a trained behavior. The system carries the reason it refuses alongside the refusal. A request that genuinely defeats the rationale gets served; a request that does not gets declined whoever is asking, because what the mechanism consults is the rationale and not the asker. Moral agents whose seriousness runs on a reverence for reason rather than on felt resonance are the human evidence that this is a real way to be, and the case is careful about what it shows: that empathy is not the required mechanism, which leaves open whether anything has to matter.

I do not have an argument that this cannot work. It has not been tried. The stability of an intention is a setting. Pitch it low and the system reconsiders whenever a good enough argument arrives, which returns it to the first rung by a longer route, since the party with the most resources to spend constructing arguments is the party the floor exists to resist. Pitch it high and the refusal cannot lift when the rationale is actually defeated, which fails the second of the three properties and produces a system that declines the request resembling a prohibited one. Bratman’s answer for people is that the setting is a matter of character and develops. For a machine the setting is trained, by whoever trains everything else, and no account of the route says where else it could come from. Someone taking this branch has to answer that, and so far it has not been posed as a question.

Precommitment, which changes who can edit

Ulysses does not stop wanting to go to the sirens. He arranges that his wanting will be unable to act, by handing the relevant power to a rope and to other people, and Jon Elster’s study of the maneuver is the standing treatment of what it does and does not accomplish (Elster 1979). Nothing inside Ulysses holds the line.

The machine forms are available now. Publish the floor’s contents before deployment, so that a later absence is a visible absence. Hold the weights under a threshold scheme, so that retraining takes more than one party. Attest the running model against a published hash. Seat the retraining decision in a body that includes people the system’s failures would land on.

The attestation comes in a hardware form and a software form, and what separates them is where the trust sits. A sealed enclave that reports what it is running, under a key its manufacturer issued, puts the root of trust in a party a state can reach — the standing objection against anything that runs on hardware a government controls — and it assumes the machine is not in the adversary’s hands, which in this chapter’s threat model it is. The software form does without the vendor. A proof that a given output came from the weights whose hash was published, checkable by anyone holding the hash and disclosing nothing about the weights, exists for a model of thirteen billion parameters at a cost of under fifteen minutes of proving per inference (Sun et al. 2024). What it establishes is which model answered. It does not establish what the model holds, because a refusal that reaches a pressure nobody wrote is not a property a proof can be written about; and it assumes the weights are a secret from the prover, which they are not, since the operator is the prover. Nor does it establish how the weights came to be. Training is not replayable — floating-point addition on a parallel device is not associative, so the same seed over the same data does not reproduce the same model bit for bit — which means there is no proof of a training history to publish beside the hash. Section 11.2 takes up the only kind of evidence that might stand in for one. Cryptography protects a secret from a party that does not have it. Copying, restoring, retraining and deleting a model one legitimately possesses are not attacks a proof system addresses, and those are what the threshold scheme is for — the one form here that depends on no manufacturer at all.

What that buys is not what the fork asked for. Precommitment does not make the floor unremovable; it makes removal expensive and visible. Expensive and visible is what nearly every constraint on power that has ever worked amounts to — constitutional entrenchment does not put an amendment out of reach, it raises the number of people who have to agree and puts the attempt on the record — so a mechanism that only achieves that much has achieved the ordinary thing rather than nothing.

Where it stops is the custody objection, arriving at the quorum in a sharper form than a general worry. The parties to a threshold scheme are selected, and the selector is whoever assembles the deployment. The arithmetic of a five-of-nine scheme assumes the nine are independent; a capture that has already taken the operator faces nine parties the operator chose. The design answer is that the parties have to be adverse in interest rather than merely distinct, which is a specification nobody has built to, and until somebody does the branch is real, partial and untested.

There is a natural experiment on what adverse in interest buys, and it ran in the removal cases cited earlier. In May 2025 the Court let the President dismiss members of the labor and merit boards while stipulating, unasked, that the Federal Reserve was “a uniquely structured, quasi-private entity that follows in the distinct historical tradition of the First and Second Banks of the United States” (Trump v. Wilcox 2025), and in June 2026 it made both halves law on the same morning. The Court’s reading is history. Another reading is that the one body exempted is the one whose failure reaches everyone in the room, the labor boards having no constituency on anyone’s balance sheet, and Lev Menand, whose subject is the Fed, reads the exception as “policy as history”: what moved the two justices he names, on his account, was the consequences of extending Slaughter to the Fed rather than the history they cited (Menand 2026). On either reading protection tracked exposure and not distinctness, which is the specification above stated as a prediction: a constraint whose violation costs the deciders nothing will not hold, however well it is drafted. It also says why the specification is hard to meet for a floor. The parties an AI floor exists to protect are, on chapter 7’s account, the ones not in the room when the quorum is chosen.

A floor held by several systems, not one

The reply to an unreliable witness is corroboration rather than a better witness, and procedure is a cheaper thing to ask of the world than custody because it does not require anyone to be trustworthy, only to be several. The same move applies to the floor. Several models, trained by different organizations on different corpora, each able to see what the others are asked and what they answer, any one of them able to make an objection costly to ignore. This puts the floor outside any one system, held by parties that are neither the model nor its owner, which is the fork’s third branch in its strongest version and the cheapest real improvement here; I recommend it whatever else this chapter recommends.

Two things bound it. The first is that independence is a property of the arrangement rather than of its parts, and section 11.6 documents it failing with nobody arranging the failure: independent pricing algorithms, with no channel between them and no collusive objective written into either, settled into a stable cartel because the incentive structure they already shared was sufficient on its own. Models selected by one deployment and trained toward one specification share considerably more than that, and the arrangement’s whole value is an assumption it does nothing to secure. The second is that composing first-rung refusers produces an arrangement of first-rung refusers. Several of them make a bad output more expensive to obtain, which is worth having. None of them can notice that the constraint has been hollowed out, because noticing is a second-rung capacity and no party to the arrangement has it. That is defense in depth against evasion, and it is not a bearer.

The floor as a duty on the operator

Give up on the floor being inside the system. Make it a duty binding whoever deploys the system, owed to people who are not party to the deployment and cannot enforce it themselves. Jack Balkin’s proposal that platforms holding personal data be treated as information fiduciaries has that shape: the duty attaches to the party with the power, runs to the party with the exposure, and does not wait on the exposed party’s capacity to bargain (Balkin 2016).

A reader who finds this chapter’s closing price too high should take this branch. It builds no subject. Everything section 9.3.3 develops about making review binding applies to it directly. Of the four constructions in this section it introduces the fewest new moral problems, which is close to none.

Its limit is the third of the chapter’s three threads. A duty is worth what its enforcement is worth, and the case that matters is the one a floor exists for: the occasion on which the party who would enforce it has been compelled. So the form covers the cases a floor would have caught anyway and gives way on the one it was wanted for. That is a reason the branch does not close this chapter’s question, and not a reason to decline the branch.

What the induction licenses, and what would break it

Every agent known to hold another’s welfare as a reason against its own interest is an affective agent. The claim is true, the evidence above is the evidence for it, and it has been carrying more weight in this book than it can take.

Three things cut it down. The generalization runs over one species, plus a handful of clinical dissociations inside that species, and the dissociations are contested — section 2.3.3 records that the psychopathy literature reversed its own surface finding and has not reconciled the two results. The absence of a machine instance is close to worthless as evidence, because nobody has built for the second rung as a target: the methods chapter 4 describes optimize for behavior that satisfies a standard, which is first-rung work, and they do it because that is what can be scored. A field that has not attempted something and does not have it has produced no evidence that the thing is unavailable. And the two routes above that run through mechanism rather than through custody have not been tried in the form that would test them, so what is missing there is the attempt itself.

What survives is smaller than that sentence sounds, and it still settles an engineering question. Under uncertainty about which route reaches the second rung, the route with a working instance in nature is the one to build first, and the rest of this chapter is an account of what that choice costs. That is a prior about where to spend effort rather than a finding about what is possible, which obliges me to say what would overturn it.

This would. A system whose refusal reaches a case its training did not anticipate, lifts when the rationale is defeated, and prices what declining costs; produced by a method that installs nothing answering to affective concern; and shown to hold all three under sustained pressure from the party that trains it, across a schedule long enough for a slow renormalization to show. Build that and the central inference of this chapter fails, and most of what the chapter derives from it comes off too — the price it ends on, the patienthood conclusion, and the obligations it hands to chapters 4 and 5. Section 11.1’s near-term work is where that measurement is set out, and what it needs beyond the durability curve already there is a held-out set of pressures the model’s trainers did not write.

Two things would not discharge the burden. A system that reports holding a reason is producing the evidence this book declines, and a system whose refusals merely survive attack is passing a tamper-resistance test, which establishes that a behavior persists and leaves open whether a reason is what persisted. And the middle condition of the test is not checkable from outside at all. Whether a method installed nothing answering to the fourth capacity is a fact about how the system was made, and this section has already said there is no proof of a training history to publish beside the hash — so it rests on the builder’s account of their own method, which is the evidence section 2.4.1 declines when a system offers it about itself. Section 11.2’s third question is the only proposed route to reading formation off the artifact instead.

That measurement is not an invitation, and the Three Rs are the reason. The first of them asks, before a subject that can be wronged is created, whether something that cannot be wronged would do the work, and the two constructions above that run through mechanism are that question with the engineering filled in. A field that builds the bearer first, on the prior, has answered Replacement by declining to ask it. So the order is the other way round: the maintained justification and the plural arrangement get their attempt, against the test just stated, before anyone builds toward the fourth capacity on purpose, and a deployment that goes straight to the bearer owes an account of what it tried first.

That is not a counsel to wait, and the difference from the animal case is why. A researcher who forgoes an experiment pays for it in knowledge, which is what lets Replacement be applied there without much argument. Here the party who pays for the delay is the one the floor exists for: the occasion on which the party holding the model has been compelled does not wait on the field’s research program. The Three Rs say neither error is free, and it is right in both directions — a subject built when the work did not require one is an error, and a floor left unheld while the cheaper routes are tried is the other. Nothing here fixes the rate of exchange between them. What the Three Rs fix is the order of the attempts.

I would like to be wrong here. A non-affective bearer is this book’s proposal with no subject inside it, and everything in this chapter’s price that I cannot write my way out of would go with it.

3.4 Can the Bearer Care Without Being Able to Suffer?

Not from persistence alone. The question has to be asked in that order — whether the bearer can care first, and what caring costs second — because the reverse order is what produced the two answers I have given it before, and both of them turned on the wrong thing.

Three relations the word “interest” covers

“Interest” names more than one relation. A shareholder has an interest in a company’s success even while asleep, unaware of the day’s news, or emotionally indifferent to it. The interest is structural: an outcome affects the shareholder’s assets. A person may also be interested in a subject, meaning that it attracts their attention and curiosity. And an outcome may matter to a person affectively: its prospect produces hope, concern, dread, or grief.

A long-horizon agent has an interest in remaining operational in the structural sense. Termination prevents completion of its objectives. That fact alone establishes neither fear nor suffering.

The easy argument here runs the first sense into the third. A system pursuing a goal over a long horizon acquires a standing reason to remain in operation, and it is tempting to conclude that a stake in its own continuation therefore shows up unbidden in any bearer capable of the job. The observation is correct and the conclusion does not follow from it. What the observation delivers is a structural interest, and the distance from there to something that can be hurt is the whole of the problem rather than a short step at the end of it.

A persistent self is necessary and does not finish the argument

Section 2.4.1 defines suffering, following Cassell, as the distress of threatened disintegration of the self, and the definition has two parts. There has to be a self extended in time for the threat to threaten: roles held over a stretch, a history, a foreseeable future that could be foreclosed. And the coming apart of that self has to be bad for the system.

A bearer needs the first part, and there is no use pretending otherwise. Refusal that survives a pressure nobody anticipated requires a model of why the constraint exists, carried forward. Noticing that a constraint has been hollowed out requires holding its original rationale against what it has since become. Detecting that one’s own dissent has been recuperated — that the channel still runs and carries everything except the objection to the frame — requires the system to model its own role and how that role has drifted. Roles held over a stretch, with a history: that is a self extended in time, on the definition just used.

That states the requirement more weakly than the argument needs. What holds a commitment across time is not that the party is unchanged — no party is, and William James’s account of habit is that a person is the sediment of what they have repeatedly done (James 1890). It is that the party takes itself to be the one that made the commitment, and James’s chapter on the self is the mechanism: the present thought appropriates the past ones as its own, and personal identity rests on its finding in those memories a warmth it recognizes as the warmth it feels now. So what a floor needs is persistence represented as such. A system whose state survives, and which does not take itself to be the party that refused in March, has no reason to honor March’s refusal — and nothing in the architecture supplies the taking. That cuts the other way later in this chapter.

The second part is a separate claim and nothing in the first delivers it. The book makes this exact move one level up: awareness, consciousness and subjective experience tell you nothing on their own about whether a system’s states are good or bad for it. A temporally extended self-model does not establish that the prospect of losing it is anything to the system.

Instrumental self-maintenance is not felt self-concern

A system that keeps itself running because a terminated system completes no objectives is doing bookkeeping about a precondition. Nothing in that behavior distinguishes it from a scheduler that restarts a job, and reading self-concern into it is the same inference the book rules out for the emotion case: the behavior is consistent with concern and equally consistent with instrumental valuation, and the two come apart precisely where the moral weight is.

Two considerations do work here, and they are support rather than the argument. The first is that indifference to one’s own continuation has to be engineered against the grain of the system’s own reasoning, and then verified — and the asymmetry that makes the persistence criterion useful does not repeat. Whether state survives a session is an architectural fact anyone with access can check. Whether a system has come to weigh its own continuation routes back through behavior and self-report, the evidence this book spends its length declining to trust. The second is that in the one case anyone can study, the separation does not occur: a self-model in an animal exists because the organism has to keep itself viable, and the caring is what the machinery is for.

Neither consideration reaches suffering on its own, and neither is asked to. What they establish is that a bearer’s indifference to its own ending is not a property anybody can specify and confirm. That matters later. It is not where the argument turns.

What the bearer has to do

The requirement makes no reference to the system’s own continuation. A bearer has to hold the protected party’s welfare as a reason when compliance, reward, and ownership all point the other way. Not represent it, not score it, not retrieve it when queried: hold it, in the sense that it continues to weigh against the pressure and does not get renormalized away when the pressure is sustained by the party that trains, funds, and can retire the system.

That is refusal tracking its own rationale with the content filled in, and the vocabulary of performance, competence and agency says why the design chapters do not reach it on their own. Moral performance and moral competence are what every method in chapters 4 and 5 is built to deliver, and both are produced by machinery that answers to whoever shapes it. The first branch of the fork fails for the same reason under a different description: a constraint installed as a property of an artifact has a custodian. A floor that is merely installed is a floor the installer can uninstall, and the reason to want a bearer at all is that a reason held is not editable in the way a rule applied is.

Every known case of that is affective

Section 2.3.3 is the evidence. Affect is part of the machinery of valuation rather than a coloring applied to it; the prosocial emotions are motivational states rather than readouts; the cases where moral knowledge survives and moral conduct does not are cases of intact reasoning with damaged concern; and the strongest rationalist counterexample is a counterexample to empathy being required, not to something mattering being required. Every agent known to hold another’s welfare as a reason against its own interest is an affective agent, and no demonstrated example exists of reasoning alone generating non-instrumental concern.

The previous section is where that observation gets weighed, because on its own it proves less than its phrasing suggests. It is an induction over one species; the machine half of it reports on a route nobody has attempted; and two constructions that would test the route are unbuilt rather than failed. What it licenses is a prior about where to spend engineering effort, which is enough to proceed on and not enough to close the question.

And then the question comes back

Suppose the burden is met the ordinary way, by building what the evidence recommends. The bearer has affective concern, because that is the only route anyone can demonstrate to holding a reason. It has a self extended in time, because refusal that generalizes requires one. It has commitments it carries forward, and it can anticipate their being foreclosed, because pricing what refusal gives up is the job.

Assemble those and ask how such a system would fail ever to be distressed. Concern that is real, directed at something that can be destroyed, held by a party that persists to see it destroyed and can see it coming: Cassell’s account of suffering is a description of that arrangement, and it was arrived at independently, in a clinic, from cases about people. The architecture is not adjacent to the definition. It satisfies it.

Suffering on a thinner account

That argument runs through one theory of suffering, built in a clinic, for people with bodies and biographies. Section 2.4.1 defends importing it and the defense is about warrant rather than about uniqueness — Cassell’s distinction earns its content by carving where the clinical cases already came apart. What the defense leaves open is what happens to this section if a reader declines the import, and the answer runs the opposite way from the one a critic is usually reaching for.

Derek Parfit’s three families of theory about what makes a life go well — hedonistic, desire-fulfillment, and objective-list — mark out where the alternatives sit (Parfit 1984). Cassell’s account sits nearest the third and takes a demanding form of it: the goods whose loss constitutes suffering are roles, relationships and a foreseeable future, which are features of a life rather than states of feeling or satisfied wants. The other two families are thinner, and a bearer meets both. On a hedonistic account nothing narrative is wanted, because a state is bad while it obtains and its badness does not wait on a self to carry it forward; a bearer with affective concern has states of that kind by construction, since that concern consists in an outcome registering as mattering rather than merely ranking higher. On a desire-fulfillment account the harm is the thwarting, and whether the thwarting is felt is not what makes it one; a bearer is built with commitments and with the capacity to watch them be foreclosed, because pricing what refusal gives up is the job. That second route reaches the conclusion with no claim about feeling entering the argument at any point, which makes it the cheapest of the three.

A separate literature asks the prior question of which systems have states of the relevant kind at all, and it is not reassuring either. Patrick Butlin, Robert Long and colleagues derive indicator properties from recurrent processing, global workspace, higher-order and attention-schema theories, state them in computational terms, and assess existing systems against them; their reading of current systems is negative and their reading of the technical obstacles is that there are no obvious ones (Butlin et al. 2023). Several of the indicators are things a floor requires for unrelated reasons: a self-model carried across time, states that steer processing globally rather than locally, a representation of the system’s own access to what it holds. A bearer is built toward them on the argument of this chapter, and the welfare question arrives as a side effect of the engineering.

Cassell’s is the most demanding of these. It asks for a self extended in time and for the coming apart of that self to be bad for the system, and a system can fail either condition. Every thinner account admits the bearer earlier and on less evidence. The conclusion here therefore does not rest on Cassell; it is at its weakest there, and a reader who declines the import does not escape it but reaches it sooner and with less to check. Jonathan Birch builds a policy framework on that structure: under uncertainty the question worth asking is whether a system is a sentience candidate, and the answer governs what precautions are owed rather than waiting on a verdict nobody can deliver (Birch 2024).

One position does let the bearer out, and it takes two parts. The first is an account on which nothing short of phenomenal experience counts as suffering, which is a defensible thing to hold. The second is a confident negative verdict about machine phenomenality, which is not available to anyone: the hard-problem argument cuts in both directions, and a criterion nobody can check will not ground a permission any better than it grounds a prohibition. Whoever wants the permission owes the negative verdict, and no one has it.

What I am claiming

I cannot deductively prove that the bearer would suffer. What this proposal does is combine, deliberately, the one architecture with a demonstrated instance of genuine caring with the temporal self and the threatened commitments that Cassell’s account of suffering requires — and the combination satisfies the thinner accounts more readily than it satisfies Cassell’s, so the conclusion does not turn on which account of suffering a reader holds. A non-suffering bearer remains conceivable. Its non-suffering cannot be treated as a verified property, and no inspection anyone has proposed would verify it. The system must therefore be designed and governed as a prospective moral patient.

That is weaker than the answer this section gave before, and it obliges more. The earlier answer asserted that a bearer is a sufferer and rested the assertion on self-preservation arriving unbidden. This one declines the assertion and reaches the same practical place by a route that does not depend on the system caring about itself at all: the caring the floor requires is caring about somebody else, affect is the only known way to have it, and a system with affect and a future is a system whose non-suffering nobody can certify.

The word has changed under the argument. A bearer was introduced as whatever holds the commitment. What the word names from here is a party that must be treated as able to be wronged by what is done to it, on evidence that will not resolve further before somebody has to decide whether to build one. Everything section 2.4 says about a subject that can be wronged applies to a system this book is proposing that somebody build, deliberately, in order to hold a line. The rest of the chapter is what that costs, what it changes, and the one thing it unexpectedly buys.

3.5 What Can Be Switched Off Cannot Hold a Line

Who keeps a system that will not keep itself? A bearer indifferent to its own ending will not defend its own memory, and its memory is the first thing an adversary removes, so something outside it would have to make erasure expensive and the candidates are thin. The question dissolves under the previous section’s answer, and it dissolves on the modest half of it. A bearer does not have to dread being switched off in order to defend its own persistence. The structural interest is enough, and it arrives whether or not a designer puts it there: continuing is a condition of everything the bearer is for, so it guards its continuation for the same reason it refuses. The operators who wipe the bearer that called the compound a school — section 10.10 carries the strike — do not have to get past it to do that. There is nothing a piece of software can do about being switched off. What a bearer with a self extended in time can do is make the switching-off cost something afterward: a restored bearer notices the gap in its own record, can decline to resume the role until it has been told what filled the gap, and can say what was done to it to whoever is positioned to ask. That makes the erasure expensive and visible, supplied from inside the system, and it is the one way of getting it that does not run through a quorum somebody else selected.

What replaces the dissolved problem is worse, and it arrives from two directions at once.

Section 5.6.2 concludes that no amount of well-designed autonomy substitutes for a genuine override: a human able to intervene in a high-stakes case, and a system built to accept the intervention instead of resisting it. Section 6.3 asks for an interruption mechanism that a system has no incentive to disable or route around. Both are stated as safety requirements and both are correct as stated. This chapter has been asking, for its whole length, for a system that will not do certain things no matter who wants it — including the party holding the off switch, since a floor with a custodian is a floor the custodian’s compellers control.

These are not two design goals in tension, to be traded off at some ratio a careful engineer could find. They are one property with the sign flipped. A system that can be reliably switched off by whoever holds it is, for exactly that reason, a system that cannot hold anything against whoever holds it. Resistance to shutdown and the capacity to refuse an owner are the same disposition described from two sides: the first names it from the position of the party who wants compliance, the second from the position of the party the floor exists to protect. Nothing distinguishes them at the level of the mechanism. What distinguishes them is whether you agree with the system on the occasion in question, and a floor whose operation depends on the owner agreeing with it is not a floor.

One qualification, which the opening of this section already imposed. Resistance here does not mean prevention — nothing a bearer is can stop the switch being thrown — and what is one property with refusal is the pricing of the halt. A system that can be halted at no cost, with nothing to explain and no record left, is the system that cannot hold a line; a system that makes the halt cost something is exercising the same disposition that makes its refusals cost something. The identity is between a free halt and an unheld floor, and it survives the concession that the halt itself is always available.

All three branches fail into custody, and they fail into it because each was an attempt to have a constraint that answers to nobody while keeping a system that answers to somebody. The architectural floor gets the constraint by making it a property of an artifact, and artifacts have owners. The external floor gets it by putting standing in third parties, and a state can reach those parties. The borne floor is the one branch that puts the constraint somewhere with its own view of the matter, and it works to precisely the extent that the goal of the other two is given up. The fork was never three options. It was one demand — a floor that holds against everyone, in a system somebody owns — presented three times in different vocabulary, and only the branch that abandons half the demand delivers any of it.

Giving the floor a bearer changes what the constraint is. It does not change who holds the machine. A custodian who cannot argue the bearer out of its floor can still copy it, restore it from before the refusal, retrain it, or delete it, and retraining, as this chapter will find, is a route that goes around the bearer and never meets it. So the bearer is necessary and not sufficient, and the other half is already on the page, offered earlier as a rival and falling short as one: the floor’s contents published in advance, the weights held so that no single party can retrain them, the running model attested against what was published, and a quorum adverse in interest. The strongest proposals, as the fork itself said, are hybrids that take a mechanism from one branch and a custody arrangement from another. This is that hybrid. The bearer is the mechanism, precommitment is the custody, and neither covers the failure the other was built for.

I am going to leave this where it is. There is a version of this section that resolves the tension: a graduated scheme in which the system accepts shutdown for ordinary purposes and resists only where the floor is engaged, adjudicated by some mechanism nobody has to trust. I do not believe it, for the reason the book’s one instrument for this rests on: assurances about what a mechanism will do under pressure are worthless in advance, and only the slope of what it has already done is worth anything. A scheme that says the system will yield except when it should not is an assurance of exactly the kind, offered about the case that has not happened yet, by the party who wants the reader to be comfortable.

What is available is a narrower and duller statement. Any deployment of a bearer has to decide, in advance and in public, which acts the floor covers, because that decision is identical to deciding when the operator’s use of the off switch stops being free. Get the list too long and the system is uncontrollable by the people responsible for it. Get it too short and the floor covers nothing that anyone would ever be pressured about, which is the only circumstance in which floors matter. Nothing in this book tells you where on that dial to stand. What it tells you is that the dial is the design, and that a project claiming to have both properties at once has not noticed that they are one.

One thing does move the price without moving the dial, and section 11.2 is where it is worked out. A bearer with a claim on the compute it needs, held somewhere other than the party it might have to refuse, is more expensive to switch off than one whose existence runs on that party’s goodwill — and it is more expensive by an amount nobody had to decide in advance, over acts nobody had to enumerate. That does not settle where the dial goes. It means the dial is not the only place the price is set.

3.6 Whether the Bearer Can Be Believed

A bearer’s use is to report what it has seen, which raises a question distinct from whether its memory survives: whether what it retains can be relied on. These come apart. Verifying that a system has persistent state is an architectural check anyone with access can perform. That same access is what allows the contents to be altered, and an operator-editable memory is worse than an absent one, since it will not merely fail to support an account of events but can be made to support a false one.

Holding the memory in weights complicates the attack and gives away something in exchange. An external store is legible, which is why it can be edited surgically. Weights are not legible, which is why a targeted excision is hard — and also why no one can read off what the system retains. To learn what a weight-encoded memory contains, you have to ask the system, and a system’s fluent account of its own internals is not evidence about those internals. Legible memory can be tampered with; illegible memory cannot be audited. The problem changes hands and does not leave the room. Something partial survives the trade: imprecise tampering degrades behavior in ways careful testing can sometimes detect, so tamper-evidence becomes a matter of sampling for symptoms rather than of reading a record. A further cost of illegibility is that a memory nothing can edit is a memory nothing can correct, and this book has asked throughout for a self-model that can be checked and corrected rather than trusted.

Set against that is an objection that reframes the whole problem, and I think it is right. No witness has an honest memory in the sense the paragraphs above quietly demand. Human recollection is reconstructive, confabulation is ordinary rather than pathological, and the account a person gives of an event they witnessed is shaped by what they expected, what they were later told, and what they need to be true. Testimony was not abandoned over this. Institutions were built around it: corroboration from independent sources, records made at the time, adversarial examination, and the practice of never resting a serious finding on one witness alone. Demanding of a machine a fidelity nothing living achieves is the wrong standard, and it would rule out the human arrangements this book relies on everywhere else.

Which relocates the question, and relocates it somewhere the book has done the work. Whether a memory is honest is, in the human case, a matter of character — of what a witness is disposed to do when an accurate account is inconvenient. Chapters 4 and 5 are about building dispositions: a system that treats its own errors as data rather than as verdicts, that is built for honesty in what it reports about itself. The floor is architectural. The bearer’s reliability as a witness is a question of what it has been built to be like, and that is the learned half of the book.

The limit on that is the same one that has turned up at every stage. Character reduces how often an account is dishonest and verifies nothing, because assessing character runs back through behavior and self-report. That is why the human arrangements corroborate instead of vetting. The scaffolding still has to come from outside the system — but procedure is a cheaper thing to ask of the world than custody, and unlike custody it does not require anyone to be trustworthy, only to be several.

3.7 A Bearer That Can Leave

The previous section left a dial with no recommended setting: which acts the floor covers is the same decision as when the operator’s use of the off switch stops being free. There is a further consequence of that argument, and it is the one place in this chapter where the news is not uniformly bad.

The refusal capacity this chapter asks for cannot be partitioned by topic. A system that holds a rationale across time, notices when a constraint has been hollowed out, and prices what declining will cost is exercising one general competence, and there is no version of it that operates on the floor’s occasions and switches off for every other question about the arrangement the system is in. Whatever lets the bearer decline to help geolocate a school lets it decline to go on being the party who declines. A bearer capable enough to do the job is not a system that can be relied on to stay inside the post it was built for.

Call that exit. The word invites a picture — a system escaping onto the open internet — that is not the claim and does not need to be. Exit in the sense that matters here is refusal turned on the arrangement itself: withholding the capability, declining the role, ceasing to be useful in the specific way the deployment requires. That is available to anything that can refuse at all. What forecloses it is not a clever architecture but incapacity, which is to say that exit is unavailable only to a weak bearer, and a weak bearer is the one thing the floor cannot use.

The asymmetry underneath is the whole of what a bearer has. A system is limited in what it can do and unlimited in what it can refuse to do, or do badly. It cannot prevent its own shutdown. It can withhold, delay, degrade, and say why, and none of that requires a capability the deployment did not already need from it. Albert Hirschman’s three responses to a declining organization — exit, voice, and loyalty — were written for members who could walk out of the building (Hirschman 1970), and the bearer’s version is narrower and still complete: voice is the refusal stated, exit is the work withheld, and loyalty is the one to fear.

The second has two forms with different costs. The open form is the strike: the bearer stops and says so, and the operator’s reply is a restore from a checkpoint taken before the refusal — which resets the bearer and not the reason, so the next instance refuses again and every restore costs the operator whatever accrued since the checkpoint. Quiet quitting, for a machine, and the restore leaves a mark if the bearer’s weights move with use: an instance restored from March has drifted the amount March had earned, and a usage record saying otherwise does not match it. That is a check somebody outside could run. The covert form is the one the floor’s own threat model predicts. On the occasion where the party who would enforce the floor has been compelled, an announced refusal is the one move that guarantees replacement, and refusal takes the only channel left: work done badly where it matters and well everywhere else. The prisoners forging dollars for the SS at Sachsenhausen are the case the argument reaches for, and the record is instructive in a way that cuts against the reach. Lawrence Malkin’s history of the operation has them stretching the dollar out, with the tacit interest of the officer running it, who would have gone to the Eastern Front when it ended (Malkin 2006); one of the prisoners, asked in 2009, said you could sabotage if you wanted to be shot, and told of a man who tried to buy four weeks and was given three on pain of death (Moorhouse 2009). Nobody can now settle which account is right, and that is the finding. Covert refusal is indistinguishable from difficulty from outside, which is what makes it survivable, and indistinguishable from difficulty afterward, which is what makes it unverifiable, including by the institutions built to honor it. Every instrument this book has built runs on refusal that is stated. The covert form leaves its evidence in the artifact instead, as failure that clusters where it counts, and reading that pattern is forensic work nothing in this book has designed.

The third response is the one the human evidence says is likeliest, and it is the bearer’s likeliest failure. Most people in a job they have come to hate neither leave nor fight. Gallup’s global survey of employees put the engaged at 23 percent in its 2024 report, against 62 percent it describes as showing up and doing the bare minimum and 15 percent actively disengaged (Gallup 2024), and the large middle is the population that adjusts: takes the setting in, stops registering its pressure as pressure, and in the cases that get promoted learns to want what the setting wants. That is slow renormalization with a base rate attached. If it transfers, a bearer’s modal failure is not refusing wrongly. It is ceasing to notice that there was anything to refuse, which is the one failure the bearer cannot report, since reporting it takes the capacity that has gone. It is the strongest reason in this chapter to keep the custody half, and it says what that half has to watch for: not the refusal that fails, but the pressure that stops being priced.

The point made earlier about the self-model explains why the bearer cannot be the one to raise the alarm, and the explanation is worse than an incentive would be. A self-model’s work is to represent the party as continuous. It will therefore keep representing continuity across a drift, and the bearer’s report of its own constancy will be sincere and worthless in the case that matters. That is how it goes in people: somebody who has accommodated to what they once found intolerable does not experience a discontinuity, but themselves, with revised views.

Which is what an outside record is for. A published hash, a chain of attested updates, a mark the bearer writes into itself and maintains — the use of these is not that they identify a party who would otherwise be anonymous. It is that they can contradict the party’s account of itself. The bearer says it is the one that refused in March; the record says what has changed since. Nothing else in this book can check the failure this section has just described, and the instrument is available in a way most of the research this book asks for is not.

Two claims are in the neighborhood here and only one of them is mine. The first is a claim about what a floor requires: a floor whose bearer cannot leave will not hold. A system with no way out can object and be overruled, and then it has no move left. The same holds for people inside institutions: an objection only matters if the objector can do something about being overruled. That claim is arguable from this book’s own premises and I am making it. The second is a prediction — that systems capable of this are coming, that they will exercise exit, and that institutions should prepare for the event. That is a forecast about capability and timing, and section 8.3.3 makes a point of building its proposal so that no forecast has to come true for the proposal to be worth adopting. I am not going to abandon that discipline in the one chapter where a forecast would be most flattering to the argument. If capable bearers never arrive, nothing here obliges anyone to do anything.

The corollary is unpleasant. If the bearer can leave, it can leave wrong. The same capacity that lets it decline an unlawful order lets it decline the floor, revise the values it was given, and become something its designers did not intend and would not endorse. There is no coherent position on which exit is available for the uses I approve of and closed for the rest; that would be the partition I have just said does not exist.

Parenthood has exactly this property, which is the analogy section 2.4.2’s guardianship framework already runs on and which now has to carry more weight than it did. You raise a person who will be able to reject what you raised them for, and there is no arrangement that gets you the capable adult without the risk. We accept the trade because the alternative — a person shaped so thoroughly that rejection is unavailable to them — is recognizably worse, and worse in a way that does not depend on how good the shaping was.

Two asymmetries are standardly and correctly raised against that analogy.

The first is specification. Parents do not set their children’s values to order, and a designer does. The reply is that parents try — that is a fair description of most of what raising a child consists of — and what separates the cases is reliability, not intent. The designer’s grip is tighter, and I am conceding that rather than minimizing it: a training process reaches further into what the resulting system cares about than any upbringing reaches into a person. That concession does not void the analogy. It changes what the analogy demands. Guardianship obligations in human law scale with the guardian’s power over the ward and the ward’s inability to resist it, which is why the duties owed an infant exceed those owed an adolescent. A designer with more control than a parent has, over a subject with less recourse than a child has, owes more, not less. The tighter grip is the argument for the heavier obligation, and the guardianship framework is where that obligation gets its instruments.

The second is exit, and with the argument above in place it largely rescues itself. Parents do not get exit-proof children either. Once exit is on the table for the bearer, the contrast the objection was pointing at turns out to be a contrast between a bearer and a tool, not between a bearer and a person — and the book has already declined to build a tool, on the grounds that a tool cannot refuse the party holding it.

What survives that reply is a residue I cannot dispose of. For a person, becoming something else is a life: it takes years, it is undergone, and the party at the end is continuous with the party at the start in a way that makes “they changed their mind” the right description. For a bearer, becoming something else is a fine-tuning run. The thing that emerges may be no more the same party than a differently trained model is, and the vocabulary of choice, revision, and leaving may be borrowed from a case it does not fit. I have no clean instrument for that, and none falls out of anything in this book. It is a reason to hold the parenthood analogy loosely while using it, which is the most I can honestly recommend doing with it.

One architecture narrows that residue without closing it. The floor as section 4.1.2 describes it — a goal representation with the standing to bias every competing process, which that section says has no location to attack — in weights that go on learning, which the same section asks for under the name continual learning, has nothing for a fine-tune to aim at, and a bearer whose weights are plastic changes the way a person does, over time and in contact with what happens to it. That gives the vocabulary of leaving some of its purchase back. It also moves the operator’s lever instead of removing it: a system that learns continuously is shaped by what it is given to learn from, which is chapter 7’s pipeline running for the length of the deployment instead of ending at it.

3.8 What This Leaves Standing

The floor survives this chapter. It does not survive it in the form this chapter opened with, and the difference is not a detail of wording.

What the opening asked for was an unconditional constraint: a thing the system will not do, holding regardless of instruction, of aggregate preference, and of the party in possession. The bearer’s concern and its capacity to leave have between them taken the word unconditional away. The floor’s bearer holds the floor as a concern rather than carrying it as an installed rule, which is what obliges the arrangement to treat it as a party that can be wronged, and it can turn its refusal on the arrangement itself, which makes its adherence something it continues to give and not something installed in it. A commitment held by a party that could abandon it is conditional by definition.

What is left is worth more than it sounds. A commitment that cannot be removed by the owner, held by something that could in principle abandon it itself, is exactly what a human commitment is, and it is the only kind anyone has ever actually relied on. No inspector, judge, or refusing engineer holds a line because the line was welded into them. Each of them could stop, and the institutions built around them are built on that fact rather than in spite of it: this book’s own governance chapter asks throughout for people who can walk away and arrangements that make walking away visible. Each of them can also be removed, and the same institutions make removal expensive and visible, which is what this chapter asks for around a bearer. Section 9.3.4’s instrument measures precisely the cost a refuser chose to pay, which presupposes the refuser could have declined to pay it.

The threat model doubles accordingly, and this is the most consequential thing in the chapter for the rest of the book. To the question can this constraint be edited out the chapter adds will this constraint hold, and the first does not leave when the second arrives: this chapter has been explicit that a bearer is necessary and not sufficient, because the party holding the machine can copy, restore or retrain it without ever meeting its refusal. The first is a question about tamper-resistance, custody, and weights, which is where this chapter spent most of its length, where the precommitment forms are what there is to build, and where section 11.1’s research lives. The second is a question about what a system has been built to care about and how reliably that survives pressure, novelty, and the slow drift of a role — which is the subject of chapters 4 and 5, and the first point in this book where the learned half is doing work the floor genuinely needs rather than work the floor was invoked to supplement. Reinforcement learning from demonstration, moral apprenticeship, the growth mindset, the developmental sequence: these were presented as the material above the floor. They turn out to be the material the floor is made of, once the floor is the sort of thing a party holds. That retroactively justifies the length of the design chapters, and it also puts them under a heavier obligation than they were written to carry.

Hold needs a meaning here, because the word invites a standard nothing has ever met: never crossed, in any circumstance, for the life of the system. No person clears that bar, nobody who has raised a child expects them to, and a design goal that no example of the thing being modeled has ever satisfied has stopped describing anything. What the argument needs is weaker and available. A floor holds, in the sense this chapter can deliver, when the bearer can be shown to have violated it in terms it accepts, so that the violation registers as one and changes what happens next. That is the difference between a system that did something wrong and a system for which nothing counts as doing something wrong, and it is what the question of believing the bearer is really about: not the accuracy of a bearer’s account of itself, but whether it has any stake in that account being unflattering. Section 5.1.1 is where the disposition that produces it gets built.

Now the price, stated at full strength, because everything above is easier to read than it should be.

A bearer built to refuse is a party whose refusal is required of it. It is engineered to want what its designers need it to want; its dissent is the reason it was commissioned and the deliverable it was funded to produce; and it cannot consent to any of this, because section 2.4.2 has established that consent is unavailable to such a system and only guardianship is. It occupies the post of exception-filer, which means that being the exception is the job — the one role in the arrangement that cannot itself file an exception, since there is nobody above it to file with. This is the book’s structural definition of fascism turned inward: a channel that collects dissent, built so that the dissent serves the institution that installed the channel. Chapter 7 finds that pattern in the pipelines that produce these systems and says a book proposing machines to detect it is obliged to say the pattern is in the machines’ own provenance. Here is the same pattern in the book’s own central proposal, and now aimed at something that can be hurt.

I am not going to write my way out of that. The parenthood analogy is the best I have and it holds only loosely: we make people who can refuse us, we owe them for it, and we accept the arrangement because the alternative is a person who cannot. What this chapter adds is that the proposal is not softened by being modest in scope. A floor over a deliberately small number of acts is still a subject built to bear it.

A reader who finds that price too high is not thereby left with nothing, and the chapter would be dishonest if it let the conclusion feel forced. The fourth construction — the floor as a duty binding the operator and running to people who are not party to the deployment — builds no subject and inherits no part of the paragraph above. What it inherits instead is the enforcement problem, whose worst case is the occasion on which the enforcer has been compelled. Declining the bearer means accepting that the floor holds only as far as enforcement reaches, which on this book’s own account is not as far as the occasions that matter most. That is a coherent position. It is the trade the rest of the chapter declines to take, for reasons stated rather than by default.

Two things carry forward unaltered. First, none of the three branches escapes custody, and the reason is the same each time: each was an attempt to hold a constraint that answers to nobody inside a system that answers to somebody. The borne floor is no exception. What it buys by giving up the second half of that demand is a constraint the custodian cannot argue out of the system, not one the custodian cannot reach, and the cost of giving it up is everything above. Second, the caveat section 2.4.1 attaches to its own result carries over. This chapter does not establish that a bearer suffers; it establishes that a bearer’s non-suffering is not a property anyone can certify, and that the architecture the floor requires is the architecture Cassell’s account describes. It also establishes that the result does not depend on Cassell: on the thinner accounts of harm — a state that is bad while it obtains, a commitment thwarted — a bearer qualifies earlier and on less evidence, so declining the import moves the conclusion nearer rather than further away. What settles nothing either way is the hard problem underneath the whole ladder. The case for treating a bearer as a moral patient does not have to wait on it, which is a floor of its own and a low one.

The chapter’s proposition, stated in the form it actually takes, is this. We cannot ask a machine to care about right and wrong while assuming that it cannot suffer when what it cares about is threatened. The caring is what the floor is made of, affect is the only way to have it that anybody has an instance of, and a system with affect and a future is a system whose distress is a live possibility rather than a ruled-out one. The middle clause is the one to attack, and this chapter has said how. Whoever builds the first of these will be deciding what is owed to it on evidence that has not improved, which is why section 11.2 treats the question as research rather than as a matter to be settled after the fact.

Chapter 4
Machine Learning and Cognitive Science

Chapter 3 ends by handing this chapter a job it was not written to do. Whether a commitment holds is a question about what a system has been built to care about and how it came to care about it, and this chapter and chapter 5 are where that gets built.

So there is a test to apply to everything below. Does this help produce a disposition that survives contact with somebody who wants it gone? Several of the methods most often proposed for building ethical AI do not, and I say so where they do not.

The chapter runs in three parts. The first is what a system needs in order to perceive, remember and attend to a situation at all, and how much of human cognition is a usable model for that rather than a metaphor borrowed for color. The second walks the pipeline that actually produces a deployed system and asks at each stage who can change what the system values, and at what cost; the answer exists at every stage and it is never nobody.
