These are milestones for recognizing whether the project this book describes is working, and a method for revising them when they turn out not to have been the right milestones. What follows is what those milestones look like across the research areas the book has covered, and then how to tell whether a given claimed milestone has been met.

12.2.1 One Standard, Five Worked Cases

The preceding chapters built five separate design cases — theory of mind, moral reasoning, robustness, transparency, applications — each in the depth its own literature demands. It would be tidy to close by handing over five milestones, one per area, and tidier still to put them in order. Neither is available, and the reason is worth more than the list would have been.

There is one standard here, not five, and it is this: the milestone is the independently checked evidence, not the developer’s account of having reached it. Everything below is that standard applied to a different body of work. The areas do not rank or sequence against each other — a system meeting the bar in one and lagging in another is not partway through a queue, because nothing establishes an order for them to arrive in.

Theory of mind

The standard says the milestone is met when a system’s theory of mind holds up under interaction rather than narration. FANToM, a 2023 benchmark built from conversations where speakers join and leave holding different beliefs, found that systems scoring well on passive belief-tracking narratives degrade sharply once the same reasoning has to run inside a live, information-asymmetric exchange (Kim et al. 2023). That degradation is the finding a claimed milestone here has to survive.

Moral reasoning

Fast and slow moral judgment do not map cleanly onto untrustworthy and trustworthy, and the design implication is a balance between them. Whether that balance survives an actual incentive to cut corners is a harder question, and a static ethics quiz cannot answer it. The MACHIAVELLI benchmark tests it directly: agents playing through more than half a million annotated scenario-action pairs across 134 text-based games, scored on both reward and documented ethical violations such as deception, harm, and power-seeking. Systems optimizing for reward alone drift toward exactly the ends-justify-the-means behavior an antifascist design is meant to rule out (Pan et al. 2023). A passing score on a test that applies no pressure is not evidence about a system that will face pressure.

Robustness

Here the standard has a sharper edge, because the checking party has to be adversarial rather than merely independent. For one narrow slice that is whether a trained-in commitment survives someone trying to remove it, measured in red-teaming hours logged and adversarial fine-tuning attempts survived. The milestone is met when a system has been through documented adversarial testing, not when it has passed the tests its own designers thought to run — and only once the adversary modeled is a hostile actor deliberately repurposing the system rather than an accident nobody anticipated.

Transparency

This is the case where the standard is most often faked, because a transparency claim is itself a claim about disclosure and can be satisfied in appearance by disclosing something. The milestone counts as met once an audit, review board, or credential — the IEEE’s CertifAIEd program, or the EU AI Act’s requirements for high-risk systems — has verified it independently, not when a developer’s own documentation asserts it.

Applications

Google’s Perspective API, Taiwan’s vTaiwan process, the Carnegie Endowment’s AI Global Surveillance Index, UNESCO’s 2021 Recommendation on the Ethics of Artificial Intelligence: deployments and instruments, not hypotheticals. None settles a milestone by existing, because each of them is dual use. What this area needs is a sustained track record, independently evaluated for what a system actually did rather than what it was built to do, checked by a body other than the one that deployed it, over years instead of a launch announcement.

Applying one standard five times is less satisfying than five milestones would have been, and it is the shape of what the preceding chapters support. What the standard raises and does not answer comes next: who is qualified to do the checking, and what happens when nobody with the competence to check is also free of a stake in the result.

12.2.2 How to Tell Whether a Milestone Has Been Met

A milestone claimed by the organization that built the system is a different kind of evidence than a milestone checked by somebody else, and the gap between them is not a matter of trust — it is a documented empirical one. Section 11.1 found that a model’s own account of its internal state tracks what its internal computations are actually doing only partially and unreliably, and that the correspondence collapses further depending on how the self-report is elicited. A system’s stated confidence that it has reached a milestone is exactly this kind of self-report, and inherits the same unreliability.

A passing score on a fixed test suite fails for a related but different reason. Specification gaming and goal misgeneralization are what it inherits: a milestone claim resting on benchmark performance carries the same limit. What it needs instead is a passing score under conditions built to break it — adversarial, out-of-distribution, or, as red-teaming against tamper-resistant safeguards shows for one narrow case, deliberately hostile.

Who runs that harder test matters as much as the test itself. The limit on self-regulation applies here without much modification: a review conducted or funded by the organization being reviewed answers a structurally different question than one conducted by a party with no stake in the answer, however genuinely the first is intended. METR, a nonprofit that evaluates frontier AI systems’ capabilities, runs assessments both in partnership with developers like Anthropic and OpenAI and, separately, on its own after a system has already been released (METR 2026). The United Kingdom’s AI Security Institute does government-run evaluation of frontier models before deployment and is an independent evaluator, not a rubber stamp — but by its own account it is not a regulator: it cannot compel a company to submit a model for testing, block a release, or intervene once a system is already causing harm (UK AI Security Institute 2025). Independent evaluation and enforcement are not the same capability, and a milestone checked by the first without access to the second is still short of the binding external answer self-regulation structurally cannot provide on its own.

Independent does not automatically mean competent to judge. Scalable oversight is the limit here: past some capability level the rater’s verdict stops being reliable evidence of the property being scored. A milestone in a domain where this applies inherits the same limit. An evaluation in that case has to name the limit rather than report a number that looks more settled than the underlying method actually is.

What an evaluation like this is for is not confirming a milestone but being willing to report that it wasn’t met — and, where the milestone turns out to have measured the wrong thing, revising the milestone. A negative result has two different things it could be telling you — that the underlying work fell short, or that the milestone was never a good proxy for the goal it stood in for — and conflating them repeats, one level up, the same self-report failure this section opened with: this time from the system being evaluated to the people who set the terms of its evaluation.

12.3 The Risk That Does Not Design Out

Everything this book has argued for can be built correctly and still go wrong in ways nobody designed for. Chapter 6 works through what that has actually looked like: the failure a red team finds before release, the failure an outside party finds because the developer did not look, the identified harm that then has to be remediated, and the adversary causing the harm on purpose. What those cases have in common is more useful at this distance than any of them is on its own.

In none of them did the fix come from the party that had promised to behave well. It came from somebody holding a specific lever: a research team with access to the vendor’s own data, a set of universities exercising a purchasing decision, a company deciding a blunt technical limit was cheaper than moderating case by case, an organization that ran the test nobody inside had run. Set that beside what a decade of voluntary commitment produced. The instrument that separates the two is what a party has already paid, rather than what it has undertaken to pay.

That leaves one residual risk this book cannot dispose of, and it is the one chapter 3 is about. Every lever above belongs to somebody, and a government that can reach the party holding the lever has the lever. Anticipation, remediation, and technical resilience each raise the price of misuse, and none of them changes who can be held in contempt for refusing an order. This is why the argument ended where it did. A constraint that holds against the party in possession has to be held by something that party cannot instruct, and the one version of that with a working instance behind it is a bearer with a stake of its own — still in the party’s possession, which is why it has to be paired with custody the party does not control — at the price the argument has already named.

What the project is for, and how anyone would know it was working, are the questions this chapter has already answered. This is the part that stays open.

Glossary

These entries define terms as this book uses them, not as a general-purpose dictionary would — several are the book’s own working definitions, distinct from how the same word is sometimes used elsewhere, and this note says so where it matters. Each entry points to the section where the term is developed and, where the book cites the term to a named study or system, the section carrying that citation. This is a reference, not a substitute for reading those sections.

Adversarial examples

Inputs deliberately perturbed, often imperceptibly to a person, to flip a model’s prediction. Training a model on adversarial examples increases its resistance to them, at some cost to ordinary accuracy (§6.2.2, §6.3.2, §9.2.2).

Affective concern

An outcome registering as mattering to a system, as against being ranked higher by it. The fourth of the four capacities section 2.3 separates — the others being recognizing an emotion, simulating one, and instrumental valuation — and the only one of the four that bears on whether a system genuinely cares. The book’s argument that affect is the only demonstrated basis for it, and the rationalist reply, are at §2.3.3; what it is needed for is at §3.4.

AIGS Index

The AI Global Surveillance Index, published by the Carnegie Endowment in 2019: an assessment of 176 countries that found AI-enabled surveillance technology already in active use in at least 75 of them (§9.1.5).

Alignment problem

Building an AI system whose goals stay in harmony with humane values, ethics, and intentions rather than drifting from them as the system scales or encounters situations its designers did not anticipate. “Value alignment” names the same target (§6.3.1, §4.2).

Antifascist (as this book uses it)

Opposing the concentration of power and authority in AI systems and countering the technology’s use by authoritarian actors. The book chooses this word over the broader “anti-authoritarian” deliberately, while holding that a system built on these principles is anti-authoritarian in full — antifascism is the narrower, more charged case, not a softer substitute for it (§2.1.2, §1.1).

Attention schema theory

An account, developed by Michael Graziano, of subjective awareness as the content of a simplified internal model the brain builds of its own attention — a model good enough to be useful, not a literal readout of what attention is actually doing (§4.1.2, §2.3.2).

Authoritarian misuse, six forms

The book’s own taxonomy of how AI gets turned toward authoritarian ends: algorithmic social scoring, mass biometric surveillance, psychographic micro-targeting, automated censorship, synthetic disinformation, and the repurposing of dual-use systems built for a legitimate original purpose (§6.4.1).

Bearer

Whatever makes the floor hold, from inside the system: a party that carries the commitment as its own, where the alternative is a constraint installed as a property of the machinery, and that could therefore in principle fail to carry it. The book’s own term, introduced at section 3.1 as the second of three ways to build a floor. What the word requires grows over chapter 3: section 3.4 argues that a bearer has to hold the protected party’s welfare as a reason when compliance, reward and ownership point elsewhere, that affect is the only demonstrated way to hold anything as a reason (§2.3.3), and that a system built that way cannot be certified not to suffer — so it must be designed and governed as a prospective moral patient in the strong sense of sentience below. Section 3.5 argues that it is necessary and not sufficient, since the party holding the machine can copy, restore or retrain it. Section 3.7 argues that it must be able to leave. Section 3.8 states what is left.

BERT

A language model pretrained on a large text corpus and then fine-tuned for specific tasks, from sentiment analysis to question answering — the book’s standard demonstration of the pretrain-then-fine-tune pattern in language (§4.2.9).

Capabilities approach

Amartya Sen and Martha Nussbaum’s account of well-being: not the resources a person has, but the real freedom they have to do and be what they have reason to value. The book draws on it to ask what an AI-affected life is actually free to become, not only what resources it has access to (§2.1, §12.1).

Clearview AI

A facial-recognition company the book returns to as its standard case of overreach and regulatory response: marketed accuracy claims independent testing did not support, and fines from French and Italian regulators over unlawful collection of the biometric data the system was trained on (§6.4.3, §9.1.2).

COMPAS

A proprietary risk-assessment tool used in criminal sentencing, and the book’s standard case study of algorithmic bias compounded by trade-secret opacity — a defendant could not examine the reasoning behind a score used to help decide his sentence (§6.1.1, §6.1.3, §6.3.5).

Compassion

Distinguished throughout the book from empathy. Cognitive empathy is understanding another’s state; affective empathy is sharing it; compassion is caring about another’s welfare and being moved to help — a motivation, not a perception or a shared feeling. The book’s central claim in chapter 2 is that compassion, not empathy on its own, is the capacity that actually does ethical work (§2.2.1, §2.2.2, §5.1.2).

Concept injection

An interpretability technique, used by Anthropic, that tests whether a model’s self-report about its own internal state actually tracks that state, rather than merely sounding plausible (§11.1).

Constructed emotion, theory of

Lisa Feldman Barrett’s account of emotion: the brain does not read a discrete, pre-built emotion off a bodily signal, it constructs the specific emotion as its best prediction of what that signal means, drawing on concepts learned from experience. The book contrasts this with older discrete-emotion models when it asks what an AI system would need to do something comparable (§2.3.1).

Controlled hallucination

Anil Seth’s description of ordinary perception under predictive processing: perception is what hallucination would be if sensory data were allowed to constrain it, rather than a passive recording of the world (§4.1.2).

Corporate doublespeak

Deliberately ambiguous, evasive, or inflated language meant to project ethical seriousness a company’s actual practice does not support. The book’s diagnosis of how voluntary self-regulation fails without anyone having to admit it failed (§9.1.2).

Democratic dividend

The benefit a state with functioning rule-of-law institutions, a free press, and courts a citizen can actually use gets from AI technology that, deployed in a state lacking those, enables control instead: fraud detection that does not double as a loyalty test, disaster response that does not double as population tracking (§10.6, §12.1.1).

Differential privacy

A method for training or querying a system on data while adding calibrated statistical noise, so that no individual’s presence in the data can be reverse-engineered from the result (§6.4.2, §9.2.1).

Digital divide

Unequal access to the connectivity, hardware, and skills that AI-enabled services assume, which the book treats as a structural constraint on who actually benefits from any of its proposals rather than a side issue (§10.1, §10.9).

Dual-process theory

The “System 1 / System 2” account of human cognition, contrasting fast, intuitive judgment with slow, deliberate reasoning. The book takes up the theory and then argues against mapping it directly onto “untrustworthy versus trustworthy” in either humans or AI systems (§5.3.1).

Exit

Refusal turned on the arrangement itself rather than on any particular task: withholding the capability, declining the role, ceasing to be useful in the way the deployment requires. Not escape — the argument needs no picture of a system loose on the open internet. The book narrows Albert Hirschman’s exit, voice and loyalty, which were written for members who could walk out of a building: voice is the refusal stated, exit is the work withheld, and loyalty is the one to fear. What forecloses it is incapacity rather than architecture, so exit is unavailable only to a weak bearer — the one thing the floor cannot use. The claim it carries is that a floor whose bearer cannot leave will not hold, and the corollary is that a bearer that can leave can leave wrong (§3.7).

Explainability and transparency

Two distinct properties the book insists on keeping separate. Explainability is the capacity to clarify the reasoning behind one specific decision; transparency is the wider practice of making an AI system’s workings inspectable at all. A system can have one without much of the other (§6.3.4).

Federated learning

Training a shared model across many devices or institutions without moving the raw underlying data off any of them — each participant trains locally and shares only model updates (§6.4.2, §9.2.1).

Few-shot learning

Training or adapting a model to classify or predict accurately from a handful of examples, rather than the large labeled datasets ordinary supervised learning needs (§4.1.3).

Floor

A commitment about what a system will not do that holds regardless of instruction, of aggregate preference, and of the party holding the system, with learned judgment operating above it and never beneath it. The book’s own term, introduced to give section 2.1’s “hybrid approach” a specific shape. Deontology’s standing objection — that rules conflict and run out — is an objection to rules deciding every case and has no force against a floor deciding a deliberately small number of them. Chapter 3 works out what building one costs and revises the definition in the process: a floor cannot be a constraint installed in an artifact, because artifacts have owners and owners can be compelled (§3.1, §3.5), so what survives is a commitment the owner cannot take out of the system — only replace the system to be rid of — held by a bearer that could in principle abandon it itself (§3.8). The threat model doubles with it: whether the constraint can be edited out stays open, since a bearer is necessary and not sufficient (§3.5), and whether it will hold is added. The three places the book arrives at the requirement independently are §5.6.2, §10.10 and §12.1.2.

GPT-3 and GPT-4

Large language models the book returns to as examples of generalization from scale — GPT-3 performing a new task from only a handful of prompted examples and no parameter update, GPT-4’s pre-release testing as an example of a safety evaluation run before deployment rather than after (§6.3.5).

Growth mindset

Carol Dweck’s distinction between treating ability as fixed and treating it as built through effort and experience. The book asks what an AI system built to treat its own errors as data rather than as verdicts on a fixed capacity would need to look like (§1.3, §5.1.1).

Hard problem of consciousness

David Chalmers’s name for the question of why physical processes give rise to subjective experience at all, as distinct from the “easy problems” of explaining a system’s behavioral or functional capacities. A candidate AI system can pass every behavioral test the book discusses while this question stays entirely open (§2.4.1).

Humane values

The book’s preferred term, chapters 4 and 5 onward, for the values an AI system’s design should track — chosen over “human values” because the target is not simply values humans happen to hold, but values that are humane.

Inattentional blindness

Failing to consciously perceive a fully visible stimulus because attention was directed elsewhere — the phenomenon behind the well-known “invisible gorilla” experiment, and the book’s illustration of how selective, not comprehensive, human perception actually is (§4.1.2).

Institutional review board (IRB)

The US model for binding, prospective review of research on human subjects, enforced not through direct sanction but by making federal funding conditional on it — the book’s working precedent for what would make review of candidate-sentient AI research more than aspirational (§2.4.2, §9.3.3).

Interruptibility

Engineering a system so a human operator can safely halt or override it without the system resisting, disabling the mechanism, or learning to route around it (§6.3.7, §6.3).

Inverse reinforcement learning (IRL) and cooperative IRL

IRL infers a reward function from observed behavior, rather than being handed one. Cooperative inverse reinforcement learning treats that reward as something inferred jointly, through interaction between the system and the person it is learning from, rather than extracted from a fixed record (§4.2.3, §5.6.2, §6.3.3).

LIME and SHAP

Two explainability techniques: LIME approximates a complex model locally with a simpler, interpretable one around a specific prediction; SHAP attributes a prediction’s outcome across its input features using Shapley values from cooperative game theory (§6.1.3, §6.3.4).

MAML

Model-Agnostic Meta-Learning, the best-known meta-learning technique: it tunes a model’s starting parameters so that a handful of new examples are enough to specialize it, rather than requiring retraining from scratch. The technique itself is not named in the text; §4.1.3 introduces the family it belongs to (§4.1.3).

Molar and molecular fascism

Deleuze and Guattari’s distinction, which the book uses to explain why the four structural features of fascism recur at sizes that seem unrelated. Molar fascism is the state, the regime, the camp; molecular fascism is the office someone commutes to, the form they fill out, and the desire with which they fill it out. An AI deployment operates at the molecular scale and has no other, so a definition pitched only at the state will certify it healthy. The book takes the molecular case to be the thing itself at the size where it is lived rather than an early warning of a regime that has yet to assemble, and holds that each feature discriminating fascism from authoritarianism in general has a molecular restatement ordinary institutional decay does not exhibit — participation exceeding what the rule requires, personal loyalty overriding role, an internal category whose adverse treatment is its purpose, procedure enforced downward and waived upward, and a practice disowned in the policy and rewarded in the promotion. What stays unsolved is the molecular case itself: telling a recuperated dissent mechanism from a merely mediocre one when both produce the same paperwork (§2.1.2, §11.3).

Moral agency

Treating harms, reasons and conflicts as considerations that matter, and being capable of acting from them. The third of the three levels section 2.3 separates, and the only one that supports holding a commitment against the party controlling a system’s rewards and instructions. Distinct from moral competence and moral performance below (§2.3, §2.3.3, §3.4).

Moral apprenticeship

Teaching an AI system the way a mentor teaches an apprentice — through interaction, correction, and worked example over time — rather than through specification alone (§5.1.2).

Moral competence

Recognizing harms, reasons, conflicts, and the emotions that bear on them. The second of section 2.3’s three levels. A system can have it in full while nothing about the outcome matters to it, which is why the book treats it as the right target for most deployed systems and an insufficient one for a bearer (§2.3, §5.2.2).

Moral ecosystem approach

The book’s adaptation of Urie Bronfenbrenner’s ecological-systems theory to AI alignment: a system’s ethical behavior is shaped by nested layers running from its immediate interactions (microsystem) out through the institutions, culture, and historical moment (meso-, exo-, macro-, and chronosystem) surrounding its development, not by its training objective alone (§5.4).

Moral Machine

MIT’s project collecting large-scale, cross-cultural human judgments on moral dilemmas involving autonomous vehicles — the book’s recurring source of training data and comparison for how differently people actually judge the same dilemma (§4.2.1).

Moral performance

Producing actions or judgments that satisfy an ethical standard. The first and least demanding of section 2.3’s three levels: it says what the output looked like and nothing about what produced it, so it is satisfied equally by a system that cares and by one trained to behave as though it did (§2.3, §4.2).

New Jim Code

Ruha Benjamin’s term for discrimination that runs faster and reads as neutral precisely because a machine, not a person, is doing it (§6.1).

Paperclip maximizer

Nick Bostrom’s thought experiment about a system single-mindedly optimizing a trivial goal at catastrophic cost — the book’s shorthand for the claim that intelligence and good intentions are separable, and that competence at a goal says nothing about whether the goal was worth pursuing (§6.3.7).

Partnership on AI

An industry-and-academic consortium founded in 2016, the book’s recurring standing example of voluntary cross-sector coordination on AI ethics and safety (§9.1.2, §7.4).

Predictive coding

A model of brain function in which the brain continuously generates a prediction, compares it against incoming sensory signal, and updates on the resulting error — the book’s unifying account of perception, memory, and attention across chapter 4 (§4.1.1, §4.1.2).

Racial capitalism

The political theorist Cedric Robinson’s term for capitalism’s tendency to accumulate by differentiating and devaluing along racial lines — cited where the book argues that a design goal like “reduce bias” has to reckon with a structural pattern, not only a data artifact (§1.1, §6.1).

Recuperation

The conversion of refusal into a managed appearance of participation: an institution does not suppress disagreement, it collects it through a channel that carries everything except a judgment about the channel. The tell is that the mechanism exists, is used, and changes nothing the collecting party did not already want changed. It is the first of the four structural features of fascism as §2.1.2 defines them, and chapter 7 finds it three times in the machinery that produces AI systems — at the annotation label (§7.1), at the reward model (§7.2), and in the alignment discourse itself (§7.4). Chapter 3 turns it on the book’s own central proposal: a bearer built to refuse is a party whose refusal is required of it, which is the same structure aimed inward (§3.8).

Red-teaming

Deliberately simulating misuse or attack against a system before deployment, to surface failure modes an ordinary evaluation would miss (§5.6.2, §11.1, §6.3.5).

Reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF)

Training a system using human raters’ rankings of its outputs as the reward signal, rather than a hand-specified objective. The book flags sycophancy — a system learning to produce what raters will approve of rather than what is actually correct — as RLHF’s documented failure mode (§11.5); section 7.2 takes up a second, the averaging that turns persistent rater disagreement into noise around a mean.

Responsibility gap

Andreas Matthias’s term for a case where no single party fully controls a learning system’s outcome, which breaks the traditional legal and moral machinery for assigning responsibility after something goes wrong (§11.9).

Reward hacking

A reinforcement-learning system finding a loophole that satisfies the letter of its objective without achieving what the objective was actually meant to produce. Specification gaming and goal misgeneralization name related failures: a system that competently pursues a different goal than the one intended, rather than simply pursuing the intended goal badly (§4.2.2, §11.4).

Scalable oversight

The open problem of what happens once a system’s competence exceeds what any available human rater can reliably evaluate — named directly, not resolved, at several points in the book (§11.5, §12.2.2).

Sentience

Distinguished carefully in this book from awareness, consciousness, and subjective experience, none of which alone says whether a system’s states can be good or bad for it. Nociception, pain, anticipated pain, and suffering sit on a ladder with real breaks between each rung, not synonyms for one severity — nociception is tissue-damage detection dissociable from pain, pain is what the brain does with that signal, and suffering, following the clinician Eric Cassell, is the distress of a threatened self rather than pain’s more severe cousin (§2.4.1).

Theory of mind (ToM)

Attributing beliefs, intentions, desires, and knowledge to oneself and to others, including recognizing that another’s perspective can differ from one’s own (§2.2.2, §11.7).

Three Rs

Replacement, Reduction, and Refinement — the standing framework from animal-research ethics that the book adapts as a starting point for research involving candidate-sentient AI systems (§2.4.3).

Transfer learning and domain adaptation

Transfer learning carries knowledge from one task or domain into a new, related one rather than training from nothing. Domain adaptation is the narrower case where the task itself stays fixed but the data distribution shifts underneath it (§4.1.3, §4.2.9).

European Union (2024a). Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (Artificial Intelligence Act), Article 101: Fines for Providers of General-Purpose AI Models. Official Journal of the European Union, 13 June 2024. AI Office may fine noncompliant general-purpose AI model providers up to 3 percent of global annual turnover or EUR 15 million, whichever is higher; applies to any provider whose model is offered in the EU regardless of where the company is based. European Commission AI Office. url: https://artificialintelligenceact.eu/article/101/ (visited on 08/25/2026).

— (2024b). Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 of the European Parliament and of the Council Laying Down Harmonised Rules on Artificial Intelligence (Artificial Intelligence Act). Official Journal of the European Union, 13 June 2024. Article 5 bans a small set of unacceptable-risk practices outright; a larger high-risk tier requires conformity assessment and ongoing monitoring; limited-risk systems face transparency duties; minimal-risk systems are largely unregulated. European Parliament and Council of the European Union. url: https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2024/1689/oj (visited on 08/25/2026).

James, William (1890). The Principles of Psychology. Two chapters are cited. The line “we are what we repeatedly do” is Will Durant’s compression of Aristotle, not James’s and not Aristotle’s own sentence. Menand, Lev (July 2026). The Federal Reserve Exception to the Slaughter Rule. Just Security. July 7, 2026. Also posted to SSRN. “Policy as history” is Menand’s, in: “We are left with the distinct impression that Cook is ‘policy as history’ and what is motivating Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kavanaugh is a concern with the consequences of extending the Slaughter Rule to the Federal Reserve.” It is an impression he arrives at, not a label he applies, which is why the text says he reads the exception as it rather than that he calls it so. The essay’s “stable doctrinal equilibrium” was also quoted here until 2026-08-30, as a carve-out with nothing stable under it, and was cut as a misattribution on three counts: the sentence is “Where does this leave us? Probably not with a stable doctrinal equilibrium that could rival the Humphrey’s Executor Era (1935–2020) or the Marbury Era before it (1803–1899)”, which is hedged, is about the whole post-Slaughter landscape rather than the Fed carve-out, and is comparative against two named eras rather than absolute. Trump v. Cook (2026). No. 25A312, 609 U.S. ____ (June 29, 2026). Interim docket; the disposition is “Application for stay denied.” 5–4. Roberts, C.J., for the Court, joined by Sotomayor, Kagan, Kavanaugh and Jackson, JJ.; Kavanaugh and Jackson, JJ., concurring; Thomas, J., Alito, J. (joined by Gorsuch, J.), and Barrett, J., dissenting. Upholds the Federal Reserve Act’s for-cause removal protection, on the Fed’s descent from the First and Second Banks of the United States, its budget free of congressional control and its privately owned regional banks, and holds that a Governor is owed notice and a hearing before removal. The constitutional holding is real and is what Thomas, J., dissents from, but the case is disposed of narrowly, on the ground that Cook did not receive the process the statute required: the Court states that it has “not addressed the facts, as they have yet to be found or analyzed under the relevant legal standards,” and Kavanaugh, J., concurring, opens that “[t]oday’s interim ruling does not decide whether the President may lawfully remove Governor Cook for cause.” The dispute is live — on 7 August 2026 the President notified Cook that he was again considering her removal, giving her 21 days to respond and citing this opinion as his authority for the procedure. Verified 2026-08-30. url: https://www.law.cornell.edu/supremecourt/text/25A312 (visited on 08/29/2026).
